title: Why Sleep Matters
hook: Sleep isn't downtime — it's when your brain consolidates memory and your body repairs itself. Skimp on it for long and the bill comes due in your health.
key_points: Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep a night for good health.
Too little sleep is linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and depression.
Sleep is when the brain consolidates memories and clears metabolic waste.
Both quantity and quality matter — fragmented sleep doesn't fully restore you.
content_html: We treat sleep like a luxury to be traded away when life gets busy. The science says the opposite: it's a biological necessity, and going short on it reliably catches up with you.
extra_html: According to the CDC, most adults need at least seven hours of sleep a night, and consistently getting less is tied to a higher risk of heart disease, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and depression. Sleep is far from passive. While you're out, the brain consolidates the day's memories, clears metabolic waste, and the body repairs tissue and regulates hormones that govern appetite and stress. Both how much and how well you sleep count — sleep that's badly fragmented by noise, screens, or apnea doesn't restore you the way solid sleep does. Treating sleep as a pillar of health, alongside diet and exercise, is one of the higher-leverage things most people can do.

source.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

related.title: What Stress Does to Your Body
related.hook: A jolt of stress is useful — it sharpens you for a real threat. The problem is when the alarm never switches off, and the body pays for staying on high alert.

flashcards.explanation_html: The CDC recommends that adults get 7 or more hours of sleep per night for the best health and wellbeing.
